claims.claim: Green light produced a much stronger signal compared to red light in intrinsic signal imaging.
claims.source: Consistent with earlier reports (Sirotin and Das, 2009; Sirotin et al., 2009), green light produced a much stronger signal.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and citations to prior work.

results.result: Computational modeling using the elastic net algorithm predicts that cross-rearing (biasing visual input to orthogonal orientations in the two eyes) causes a shift of OP pinwheels towards OD borders. The model shows that as the strength of over-representation (α) increases, pinwheels shift away from OD centers, with both pinwheel positions and OD borders moving.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C13-C16, C64-C67 collectively demonstrate that the elastic net model successfully predicts pinwheel repositioning under cross-rearing conditions. The computational results are internally consistent, showing dose-dependent effects (Figure 1) and mechanistic explanations for the spatial reorganization. The model parameters and methodology are adequately described.

results.result: Cats were reared from 3 weeks of age wearing -10 dioptre cylindrical lenses (vertical axis on left eye for horizontal orientations, horizontal axis on right eye for vertical orientations) for 6 hours daily. Five cross-reared animals (10 hemispheres) and 6 control animals (11 hemispheres) were studied using optical imaging and electrophysiology from age 20 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 describe the experimental design with appropriate detail. The lens strength was justified by preliminary behavioral observations (C20), and sample sizes are clearly stated (C22). The methodology appears sound, though the relatively weak lens power (-10 dioptres) compared to prior studies is noted.

results.result: Single-unit recordings from cross-reared animals (182 units from 20 tracks) showed orientation preference distributions biased toward the experienced orientations for each eye, well-fit by sine curves with 180° period (r²=0.75 left, r²=0.79 right). Control animals (86 units from 17 tracks) showed cardinal orientation over-representation fit by 90° period sine curves (r²=0.69).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 present electrophysiology data with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 3a,b). The r² values indicate good model fits, and the results are consistent with the experimental manipulation. Sample sizes are adequate for single-unit studies, though electrode placement was not guided by map structure.

results.result: Both control and cross-reared animals showed significant torsional disparity in preferred orientation between eyes (ΔOP = 11.7° and 9.8° respectively, both p<0.001), with no significant difference between conditions (p=0.44).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 report appropriate statistical tests (two-tailed t-tests) with significant p-values for within-group comparisons and non-significant between-group comparison. This finding is consistent with prior literature and suggests the manipulation did not alter basic binocular disparity properties.

results.result: Cross-reared animals showed significantly higher monocularity (median MI=0.38) compared to controls (median MI=0.24, p=0.002, Kruskal-Wallis test).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 present a statistically significant difference using an appropriate non-parametric test (Figure 3c). The effect is modest but consistent with the experimental manipulation creating some degree of eye-specific tuning while maintaining substantial binocularity.

results.result: Cross-reared animals exhibited marginally higher preferred spatial frequencies (median 0.24 vs 0.16 cycles/°, p<0.001) but no differences in bandwidth (p=0.19) or skew (p=0.40) of spatial frequency tuning compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 report statistically significant differences in preferred spatial frequency but acknowledge substantial overlap in tuning curves (Figure 3d). The lack of differences in bandwidth and skew suggests the effect is subtle. Appropriate statistical tests were used.

results.result: No significant differences were found between control and cross-reared animals in temporal frequency tuning (p=0.2), temporal frequency bandwidth (p=0.28), temporal frequency skew (p=0.63), maximum spike rate (p=0.56), or semi-saturation contrast (p=0.81).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 report multiple non-significant comparisons using appropriate statistical tests. These negative results suggest that basic response properties and contrast sensitivity were preserved in cross-reared animals, supporting the interpretation that the manipulation specifically affected orientation processing.

results.result: Green light (520 nm) imaging provided higher signal-to-noise ratio than red light for intrinsic signal imaging. Extended spatial decorrelation (ESD) successfully removed blood vessel artifacts from green light data. Maps from green and red light were highly correlated (r²=0.78 for OP, r²=0.77 for OD), and imaging-derived orientation preferences correlated well with electrophysiology (r²=0.64, p=0.003).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42, C71-C72, C80-C82 present methodological validation with appropriate quantitative comparisons (Figure 4). The high correlations between imaging modalities and between imaging and electrophysiology support the validity of the green light/ESD approach. The median absolute difference of 15.2° between methods is reasonable.

results.result: Optical imaging revealed that control animals showed cardinal orientation over-representation (90° period sine fit, r²=0.6), while cross-reared animals showed orientation distributions biased toward lens orientations for each eye (180° period sine fits, r²=0.64 left, r²=0.71 right). Cross-reared hemispheres had slightly lower median orientation selectivity (p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47, C79 present optical imaging data consistent with single-unit recordings (Figure 5). The r² values indicate good model fits, and the results match the experimental manipulation. The small but significant reduction in orientation selectivity (C79) is appropriately noted as subtle despite statistical significance.

results.result: Cross-rearing did not significantly change pinwheel density or the distribution of intersection angles between OD and OP maps. However, subtle changes in orientation selectivity distribution were observed: selectivity was slightly greater near OD borders in controls but near OD centers in cross-reared animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 report both negative results (pinwheel density, intersection angles) and subtle positive findings (selectivity distribution). The negative results are important controls showing that basic map structure was preserved. The selectivity distribution change (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) is appropriately characterized as subtle.

results.result: In cross-reared animals, pinwheels showed a significant shift away from OD centers compared to controls, with significant under-representation in the center bin (p=0.01, power=0.77, 95% CI [0.06, 0.36]). Control animals showed pinwheel distributions similar to prior literature (Hübener et al. 1997).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 present the key experimental finding with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 6b,c). The two-tailed t-test with reported power and confidence interval is appropriate. The effect matches the computational prediction, and the control data validates the methodology by replicating prior findings.

results.result: The experimental results confirm the computational prediction that cross-rearing causes pinwheel repositioning relative to OD columns. This demonstrates that the spatial relationship between OP and OD maps can be modified by visual experience, revealing previously unknown cortical plasticity and supporting dimension reduction models of map development.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C55, C63, C76-C77 present the main conclusions of the study. The agreement between computational predictions and experimental results is strong (compare Figures 1 and 6). The claim of 'previously unknown plasticity' is justified given prior failures to modify this relationship. However, the broader claims about 'redefining limits of plasticity' (C76) are somewhat overstated.

results.result: The findings agree with prior stripe-rearing studies showing orientation-specific over-representation. Unlike studies with stronger biases where cells became monocular, only ~10% of units were monocular in cross-reared animals, suggesting relatively normal binocular summation and access to sufficient orientation range for binocular fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 appropriately contextualize the results within prior literature. The comparison with stronger lens studies is valid, and the inference about binocular function (C58-C59) is reasonable given the monocularity data, though somewhat speculative since binocular function was not directly tested.

results.result: Prior theoretical work predicted pinwheel movement and annihilation during development, but chronic imaging studies suggested pinwheels don't move with normal visual input. However, electrical microstimulation studies in adults showed pinwheel rearrangement.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 accurately summarize prior theoretical and experimental work on pinwheel dynamics. The citations are appropriate and the apparent contradiction between theory and normal development observations is correctly noted, providing context for the current findings.

results.result: The relatively weak lenses used (-10 dioptres vs 67-167 dioptres in prior studies) suggest visual cortical structure is sensitive to small variations in sensory input. This raises the possibility that individual variability in map structure could partly reflect variations in visual experience, including naturally occurring astigmatism (up to 6 dioptres).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 make a reasonable inference about cortical sensitivity, but C75 is highly speculative. While the comparison with astigmatism is interesting, there is no direct evidence linking natural visual experience variations to map structure differences. This would require longitudinal studies or correlations between individual visual experience and map structure.

results.result: Prior work established that individual OP and OD maps can be modified by altered visual input, but the spatial relationship between them (particularly pinwheel location relative to OD centers) has appeared immutable. Dimension reduction models predict this relationship might be sensitive to visual experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C6-C12 accurately summarize established knowledge and prior theoretical predictions. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of the field's understanding (immutability of map relationships) correctly sets up the study's contribution. The description of dimension reduction models is accurate.

results.result: The degree of plasticity of V1 neurons depends on their position in the OP map (pinwheel vs iso-orientation domain), though the direction of this dependence is controversial between studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 accurately describe a controversy in the literature regarding position-dependent plasticity. The citations to conflicting studies (Dragoi et al. 2001 vs Schuett et al. 2001) are appropriate. This provides relevant context though it's not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: In cats, both areas 17 and 18 receive direct input from the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and are therefore both primary visual cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 correctly describes cat visual cortex anatomy with appropriate citation. This justifies the inclusion of both areas 17 and 18 in the analysis, which is important for the study design.
